newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Elderly should not be denied radiotherapy - study.
newsitem.headline: Elderly should not be denied radiotherapy - study.

text.p: Elderly cancer patients are being denied radiotherapy because of a misconception that older people cannot tolerate the treatment, according to a new study presented by cancer experts on Wednesday.

Speaking at an international conference on cancer in Vienna, Pierre Scalliet, Professor of Radiotherapy at Belgium's Cliniques Universitaires St-Luc, said the study showed patients should be evaluated on their state of health, not their age.
"A heavy drinker and smoker aged 40 will be much less healthy than many 80-year-olds. Age by itself is not a basis for selecting treatment," he told Reuters.

The study involving some 13,000 cancer patients in Europe aged between 40 and 80 provided the first data showing no major difference in the way old and young people responded to radiotherapy, he said.
Patients with thoracic, pelvic and head and neck cancer were monitored in 20 trials by the European Organisation for Research and Treatment of Cancer (EORTC).
Survival was comparable in each age group, and only older patients who received thoracic radiation suffered greater toxicity, or side-effects, than younger patients.
"But this was temporary and not significant -- certainly no reason to differentiate between age groups," Scalliet said.
He said the number of cancer patients would rise dramatically in the next 10 years as more people in Europe reached old age, and doctors needed to be prepared to cope with the change.
"Cancer is a time-bomb as far as infrastructure and medical training is concerned," he said, noting the number of cancer patients was likely to increase by around ten percent by 2007.
"We need to be able to plan ahead or we won't be able to cope with the increase. There are enough doctors but not enough specific training in the treatment of elderly patients," he added.

Cancer experts on Monday told delegates at the four-day European Society of Therapeutic Radiology and Oncology conference that about half of all cancer patients survive and that 40 percent of those have received radiotherapy.
But despite the evidence, doctors in Europe generally remained cautious about recommending radiotherapy and were unaware of its benefits, they said.
"Radiation is a well established treatment already responsible for saving five million Europeans alive today," said Jens Overgaard, Professor of Oncology at Denmark's Aarhus University.
